title: Pauri 25, meaning: even hunger is a gift
hook: His generosity cannot be written; even pain and hunger are counted among His gifts (Japji 25)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sound of Pauri 25. Your line was bahutaa karam: generosity too great to write down. Did you give one thing without keeping score? Today, the hardest line in the stanza. Day two hundred four.

Ask someone about the worst year of their life, and then ask what came out of it. Sometimes there's a pause, and then something surprising. That's when I learned who my real friends were. That's when I stopped drinking. That's when I found out I could survive. Nobody chooses a year like that. Some still wouldn't give back what it taught them. Pauri 25 says something about hard things that is easy to misunderstand, so let's go slowly.
screen: `THE WORST YEAR OF YOUR LIFE.` → `WHAT CAME OUT OF IT?` → `GO SLOWLY HERE.`

segments.voice: Today's word is daat: a gift, something given. Pauri 25 began: His generosity is so great it can't be written. Then it looks at everyone receiving, in paraphrase. Many great warriors come begging at the Giver's door. Countless others, beyond counting. Some waste away in their own vices. Some take and take, then deny they ever received. Some fools just keep on eating. And then the line: so many endure pain, hunger and constant blows. In the original: eh bhi daat teree daataar. Even these are Your gifts, O Giver. Now, what does that mean, and what doesn't it mean? It doesn't mean hunger is fine, or that the hungry deserve it. Sikh life answers hunger by feeding people; that's what yesterday's langar is for. It doesn't tell anyone in pain to be quiet. What it says is that even the hard things come from the same hand, under the same Hukam, and can carry something in them. Guru Nanak says it elsewhere, in the Asa di Vaar, in paraphrase: pain can be the medicine, and comfort the sickness. The stanza goes on: release from bondage comes by the divine will; no one else has a say. The Giver knows, and the Giver gives. And the last lines: the one who is blessed to sing praise, Nanak says, is the king of kings. So the stanza ends not on wealth or even comfort, but on the gift of praise, which can come even in a hard year.
screen: `DAAT — A GIFT.` · `EH BHI DAAT TEREE DAATAAR.` · `NOT: HUNGER IS FINE.` · `PAIN AS MEDICINE.` · then, large: `EVEN THIS IS A GIFT.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one difficulty, not the heaviest thing you carry, just something hard in your life right now. Hold it gently. Don't pretend it's good. Then ask quietly: is there anything inside this, something it's teaching me, someone it's brought closer, a strength it's showing? If you find one small thing, rest with it. If you don't, that's all right too; just breathe with the difficulty. The bell holds the time.
Daat. A gift. Pauri 25 counts even pain and hunger among the Giver's gifts, and ends on the gift of praise.
Your line: even this is a gift. Today, when something small goes wrong, ask once whether anything is hidden in it, and don't force an answer. Day two hundred four.

howItsDone: Pauri 25 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; many Sikhs speak of accepting the bhaana, the divine will, in hard times, while also serving in the langar to feed the hungry.

fork.setup: you're going through pain and hunger. what does Pauri 25 call it?
options: even this is Your gift, O Giver.
fork.reveal: eh bhi daat teree daataar. not that hunger is fine, but that even hard things come from the same hand and can carry something.

original.note: Gurmukhi: daat, a gift; daataar is the Giver. Japji Pauri 25: eh bhi daat teree daataar.

trapdoor: what you thought: suffering is good for you.
what it means: even hardship comes from the same Giver and can carry a gift, without anyone pretending it's easy.
what a scholar hears: daat and daataar share a root; the Asa di Vaar says pain can be the medicine and comfort the sickness; the stanza closes: the one given praise is king of kings.
